title: Don't Expect to Get It Right in One Draft: Good Scripts Are Made in the Rewrite
excerpt: The real writing happens in the rewrite. Paul Chitlik's advice is practical and constructive, and it is useful not only to screenwriters but to anyone struggling with a piece of writing — in theater, in fiction, anywhere.
body:
The real writing happens in the rewrite. Paul Chitlik's advice is practical and constructive, and it is useful not only to screenwriters but to anyone struggling with a piece of writing — in theater, in fiction, anywhere.

## About the Author

Paul Chitlik is an American screenwriter, producer, and director who lives in Burbank, California. He has written feature outlines and screenplays for Nu Image, Rysher Entertainment, Mainline Releasing, Promark, and others. He has been nominated for a Writers Guild of America Award and a GLAAD Media Award, and he has won a Genesis Award.

He has produced a number of film and television works, chiefly the film *The Wedding Dress*; the series *Who's the Boss?*, the new *Twilight Zone*, *Brothers*, *Small Wonder*, *Amen*, *Perfect Strangers*, and *V.I.P.*; and the TV movie *Alien Abduction*. He also teaches, and has given screenwriting courses at UCLA, Loyola Marymount University, the Escola Superior de Cinema i Audiovisuals de Catalunya (ESCAC), and the film school at the University of Barcelona in Spain, among other places.

## Foreword to the Book

Every professional screenwriter — and most amateurs with any real experience — knows that no script has ever gone into production on its first draft. Before a script reaches the shooting stage, a dozen or twenty rewrites are nothing unusual (one of my own projects went through thirty), and even then it isn't finished. Most professional screenwriters have the benefit of expert guidance close at hand: other writers, executive producers, producers, development executives, agents, managers. These people will do almost anything to help a writer survive the rewrite. New writers get none of that. They have no professional system to carry them from the "vomit draft" to a piece of work with the polish to show someone.

Beginners just entering screenwriting can turn to Syd Field's *Screenplay*, Richard Walter's *Screenwriting*, or Chris Vogler's *The Writer's Journey*. There are at least twenty books you could use to learn the basics; I list only those three. But when it comes to the actual work of rewriting, only a handful of books are any help at all. It is fair to say that no book suits the beginner — none gives him concrete, practical, step-by-step instruction; none offers a complete, usable method to walk him through the whole process. Some film schools that teach a rewriting course (few schools do) have been stuck without a textbook, and some instructors have had to write their own.

*Rewrite* is a practical guide for beginning screenwriters, one that can carry you to your next draft. **From assessing your own script to tearing it down and rebuilding it, the book lays out a course of specific, easy-to-follow tasks that takes you through the miasma of the rewriting stage.** The film examples are all drawn from movies everyone knows, and exercises come at regular intervals. With this book beside you, the hard journey of the rewrite is a little less lonely, less anxious, less aimless. It works like a development executive at your elbow, a teacher, a trusted advisor; when you cannot get direct feedback from an audience, this book will guide you through the rewrite.

Over twenty-five years as a film and television writer, producer, and director, and eight years teaching at UCLA and Loyola Marymount University, I have rewritten hundreds of television scripts and screenplays — literally hundreds — and if you count the scripts I have coached and the rewrites I have done for others, add another 700. The first thing I learned about screenwriting is that writing is hard. The second is that if you don't rewrite what you've written, it isn't done. Yes, the torment of getting the script onto paper, the torment of the blank computer screen, ends the moment you finish the first draft. You can sit back in your chair and feel the warmth of "it's finished" spread through you. The trouble is that you are unsure of yourself, or unsure of the process, and you don't know what to do next — which is why every drawer in the house is stuffed with manuscripts that may never see daylight again.

But now it is time to take that unpolished diamond — this block of granite you have already cut out of the quarry in your head — and turn it into the Star of India, or the *Pietà*. Or let's drop the comparison: you are going to have to recycle the ink and paper of that first draft, because as it stands you probably can't sell it. Rewrite it and you might just turn it into *Chinatown* (1974) or *Shakespeare in Love* (1998).

Look at it from another angle. Every year more than 55,000 scripts are registered with the Writers Guild of America, West, while the studios and production companies (and I don't mean that friend of yours who just bought a high-definition digital camera) make only about 350 films. And I can tell you I am absolutely certain that not one of those 350 films is a genuine first draft. Every one of those scripts was rewritten by its original author at least once, usually a dozen or twenty times, and very likely other people joined in as well. So the fact is that to become one of the 350 out of 55,000, you have to pass through that stronghold called "Rewrite."

Rewrite Town is not such a wicked place, actually. To quote the writer-director Jane Anderson: "Your first draft is inevitably going to be bad." She even suggests that you deliberately write it a little "badly," because "that's not a flaw, it's part of the process."

You may even find you enjoy it. As my friend Vince McKay says: "The magic begins." Or as one of my students put it: "This is where the work starts." Only in the rewrite can you produce the lines that turn rot into gold; only in the rewrite can you stop merely narrating plot and information and put your strength into making characters leap off the page. Jim Schmerer, who ran UCLA's online professional program in screenwriting, has a television résumé that runs from *Star Trek* (1973) to *MacGyver* (1985) — far too much to list. Jim once used a moment from *Outbreak* (1995, written by Lawrence Dworet and Robert Roy Pool) as an example. The film needs the character played by Dustin Hoffman to get information out of the Coast Guard, and his secretary tells him she has a friend in the Coast Guard. In the first draft Hoffman said: "Can you ask him for help?" — and he got all the information he wanted. In the final draft he says it differently: "How good a friend?" The secretary answers: "Better than he is with his wife." That one line tells us two things: that she can get the information, and something about who she is.

You can only create a one-two punch like that in the rewrite, because when the first draft has you tied in knots, you have no attention left for it.

But the process takes many, many drafts. Now it is time to see whether everything in your head has actually made it onto the page; time to chip off every piece of that block of granite that isn't part of the *Pietà*; time to sand and polish, stretch and compress, build and shape your script. Better still, the page in front of you is no longer blank. Rewriting takes thought and it takes craft — but if you have no mentor, no studio executive, no director to give you a few tips, where do you start?

Start with this book. Put your script on one side of the desk and this book on the other. You will follow a clear process, one that helps you analyze your own script, tell the strong parts from the weak, and draw up a plan and a blueprint for the rewrite.

There is an old line about screenwriting: rewriting is hard. Rewriting on your own is harder. Having *Rewrite* is like having a personal rewriting coach; you don't have to get through the whole thing alone. Every chapter sets practical exercises that bear directly on the script in front of you and also give you methods you can use on future scripts. You will get the most out of them by doing them as you rewrite. You can also read the book straight through before you write anything new.

The order of this book is the order I recommend to my students, but every beginner comes at the rewrite from a different angle and will naturally do things in a different order. So read and use the book however suits you.

There is one rule in screenwriting: there are no rules. Some methods have been around for a hundred years (2,500 years, in playwriting), but there are no rules. So if you disagree with something I say, follow your own instinct and see whether it works. If it does, good. If it doesn't, try my way and see how it turns out. There's a fair chance my way will work, because it isn't mine: it is how most screenwriters and most Hollywood development executives handle scripts today.

Let me answer one more question. What we are discussing here is Hollywood movies, not films like *Jules et Jim* (1962), *Shoot the Piano Player* (1960), *Los Olvidados* (1950), *Belle Époque* (1992), or the "Apu Trilogy" (*Pather Panchali* [1955], *Aparajito* [1956], *The World of Apu* [1959]). Some of what I have to say works for those films too, but not all of it. I don't know how to write a screenplay for the French New Wave, for Italian Neorealism, for Spanish films before and after Franco, or for Indian films after independence — good films that have moved their own countrymen deeply, and have even moved us crude Americans. But in fairness, to most American audiences these films are foreign and unfamiliar in structure, method, and content, which is why most Hollywood studios and production companies won't take them. The goal I have assumed throughout is a film an American studio might buy and an American audience might enjoy.

Even so, if your goal is to make the best independent film outside Hollywood, you will still need my methods to rewrite it better, rather than straining to copy the pattern of *Last Year at Marienbad* (1961). (If you can work out its pattern, wonderful. I can't, not even after reading the novel.) A good independent film still needs good structure, good characters, good dialogue, good action.

So let's start rewriting.

But wait. How long will this take? If you have nothing else on and can give all your time to it, a few weeks to a few months. If you also have a job and a family and can put in ten hours a week, perhaps three or four months. The hours depend on your own situation.

Screenwriters are notorious procrastinators. Whatever you do, I recommend making a plan. I regularly clean my office, vacuum the house, go for a bike ride, and then drop the dirty laundry at the cleaners. Whatever it is you are going to do, write it down, then do it. Don't keep adding to the list, and when you have finished what's on it, get ready to start rewriting. Clear head, ready mind. Then: welcome to Chapter One.

A Note on Gender

To avoid confusion, when I write about a character in a film I generally use male pronouns. When I mean a female character specifically, of course, I use female pronouns. And when I refer generally to readers, producers, writers, development staff, agents, and studio personnel, I use male pronouns as well. Any of those jobs, of course, is held by women as well as men.
